context: MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. Prior to 8.6.5, an unauthenticated reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in OGC API Features collection-items HTML output allows crafted offset or limit query parameter values from raw CGI request handling in src/mapogcapi.cpp to reach template.params.offset or template.params.limit. share/ogcapi/templates/html-bootstrap/collection-items.html inserts those values without quoting or escaping into a script element. A victim who follows a crafted request can have the script element terminated by attacker-controlled markup, causing arbitrary JavaScript to execute under the MapServer origin and enabling access to browser-session data, actions as the victim, and content manipulation. This issue is fixed in 8.6.5.

context: MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. From 4.4.0 until 8.6.5, an unauthenticated remote attacker can send a WCS GetCoverage XML POST request whose BoundingBox element omits the crs attribute, causing xmlGetProp() in src/mapwcs.cpp to return null. msWCSParseRequest() then calls string functions on the null value before normal WCS exception handling, crashing the CGI or FastCGI worker. The analogous KVP or GET path is not affected because it obtains a count-validated, non-null token. A single request can terminate one worker, and repeated requests can exhaust a fixed worker pool and deny service. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

context: MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. From 6.0 until 8.6.5, MapServer's WMS OpenLayers output, selected by FORMAT=application/openlayers or template=openlayers, substitutes a request-derived online-resource value into a single-quoted JavaScript string in src/maptemplate.c. The prior remediation for GHSA-xqj6-vjqr-33vv used msEscapeJSonLikeString() to protect the JavaScript string but did not neutralize angle brackets, so attacker-controlled X-Forwarded-Host or X-Forwarded-Proto values can still terminate the script element at the HTML parser layer. Deployments that expose attacker-controlled PATH_INFO or map= values reaching the same string are also affected. An unauthenticated attacker can cause arbitrary JavaScript to execute in a victim's browser under the MapServer origin when the victim loads the crafted output. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

context: MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. From 8.2.0 until 8.6.5, an unauthenticated attacker can send a WMS GetLegendGraphic request with a nonempty BBOX and repeated LAYER parameters to trigger a heap buffer overflow in msWMSDispatch() in src/mapwms.cpp. The handler appends synthesized entries to cgiRequestObj.ParamNames and cgiRequestObj.ParamValues at NumParams without retaining the arrays' capacity or reallocating them, while incrementing NumParams inside the loop. Once the parser's hidden capacity is exhausted, the writes pass the heap allocation boundary. A single request can corrupt heap memory and crash the process; code execution may be possible but was not demonstrated. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

context: MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. Prior to 8.6.5, MapServer's MySQL JOIN implementation in src/mapjoin.c copies the source layer attribute selected by JOIN ... FROM into joininfo->target and inserts it into the query built by msMySQLJoinNext() without parameterization or SQL escaping. When MySQL JOIN support is enabled, an attacker who can control that source feature attribute, including through imported shapefile or DBF data or another untrusted spatial source, can inject SQL operators or expressions that change the intended JOIN predicate. This can bypass the intended key comparison and expose unrelated records from the MySQL or MariaDB JOIN table through output templates, query responses, or downstream application logic. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

context: MapServer is a system for developing web-based GIS applications. Prior to 8.6.5, MapServer's PostgreSQL JOIN implementation in src/mappostgresql.c copies the source layer attribute selected by JOIN FROM into joininfo->from_value and embeds it without parameterization or escaping into a dynamically generated PostgreSQL query executed by PQexec(). When PostgreSQL JOIN support is enabled, an attacker who can control that source feature attribute can inject quote characters and SQL operators that alter the intended WHERE predicate. This second-order injection can cause unintended rows and JOIN attributes to be returned, potentially exposing information from unrelated PostgreSQL records. This issue is fixed in version 8.6.5.

context: Tapo provides Rust and Python APIs and an MCP server for TP-Link Tapo smart devices. From 0.3.1 until 0.5.0, the Streamable HTTP implementation in tapo-mcp/src/server.rs calls disable_allowed_hosts() without replacement Host or Origin validation, while TAPO_MCP_API_KEY remains optional for a listener that can bind to all interfaces. A malicious website can use DNS rebinding to send same-origin browser requests to the victim's local or LAN Tapo MCP listener when it runs without an API key. The attacker can invoke exposed tools including control_device for smart-device actuation and take_snapshot for configured cameras. Deployments with TAPO_MCP_API_KEY set are not affected by the unauthenticated path, and exploitation requires a running listener configured with real Tapo credentials and devices, plus victim interaction with the malicious site. This issue is fixed in version 0.5.0.

context: memtomem-stm is a short-term memory proxy gateway with proactive memory surfacing for AI agents. From 0.1.2 until 0.1.34, concurrent surfacing RPC failures can start more than one reconnect for the same dirty session because concurrent LTM recovery is not uniquely owned by a session generation. Cancellation during a post-reconnect retry can also leave the replacement transport reusable after an interrupted protocol exchange, causing session-state integrity loss or local service degradation. The duplicate-reconnect subcase was introduced in 0.1.24, while the cancellation-recovery subcase affects the broader listed range. This issue is fixed in version 0.1.34.

context: memtomem-stm is a short-term memory proxy gateway with proactive memory surfacing for AI agents. From 0.1.0 until 0.1.34, untrusted long-term and working-memory fields can introduce Markdown or HTML-compatible structure into the surfaced-memory envelope because those fields are not serialized as inert data. A crafted memory can create misleading structural boundaries or visually conceal surfaced content, affecting how a consuming agent interprets the memory context. Ordinary natural-language persuasion remains a residual model-level risk and is outside the structural serialization flaw. This issue is fixed in version 0.1.34.

context: Pozeiden is a MermaidJS renderer written in Zig. Prior to 0.3.0, Pozeiden emits attacker-controlled Mermaid values into SVG attributes or markup without sufficient XML escaping or URL scheme validation, and first-party consumers such as zigmark and policypress embed the generated SVG raw into HTML. The click href syntax can introduce a dangerous URL scheme or break out of an attribute; style, classDef, ::: class assignment, and linkStyle color values can inject fill or stroke markup; color and font-weight values can escape text attributes; %%{init}%% themeVariables can inject global renderer attributes; and quadrant y-axis labels can introduce raw markup. These paths involve src/svg/writer.zig, src/renderers/flowchart.zig, src/renderers/quadrant.zig, and src/root.zig. An attacker who can influence rendered Mermaid source can therefore store script-bearing SVG that executes when another user views the published HTML. This issue is fixed in version 0.3.0.

context: Pozeiden is a MermaidJS renderer written in Zig. Prior to 0.3.0, src/renderers/c4.zig, src/renderers/class.zig, src/renderers/er.zig, and src/renderers/requirement.zig use fixed row-layout arrays while deriving subsequent loop bounds from an untrusted diagram's actual item count, and src/renderers/state.zig indexes a fixed depth array using user-controlled nesting depth. A valid diagram with at least 193 grid items can make the row count exceed the 64-row storage, while a deeply nested state diagram can exceed the col_count depth storage through the public pozeiden.render() path. Safe CLI and ReleaseSafe builds abort the rendering process, enabling reliable denial of service in applications that render untrusted diagrams. ReleaseSmall WASM builds with safety checks disabled instead perform out-of-bounds stack reads or writes, creating a memory-safety violation. This issue is fixed in version 0.3.0.

context: pmo-platform is a modular PMO and release-management platform for Claude Code. From 3.48 until 3.69.1, release/skills/pmo-skill-refiner/eval-viewer/generate_review.py reads untrusted model or skill output from workspace/run*/outputs/ and embeds it with json.dumps into viewer.html inside an inline script without escaping HTML metacharacters. A crafted output can close the script element and execute JavaScript when an operator generates and opens the viewer. The maintainer also confirmed that DOM-based injection through renderGrades and renderBenchmark innerHTML survives transport-only escaping, so affected render sinks must neutralize the content. Executed script can read embedded prompts and outputs, alter the viewer DOM, or modify saved feedback. This issue is fixed in version 3.69.1.

context: pmo-platform is a modular PMO and release-management platform for Claude Code. Prior to 3.69.1, core/hooks/block-credential-reads.sh, core/hooks/block-egress.sh, core/hooks/block-fs-boundary.sh, and core/hooks/block-mcp-writes.sh pin PATH to /usr/bin:/bin, hard-code jq as /usr/bin/jq, and return success when jq is unavailable there. On systems where jq exists only in a Homebrew path, including affected pre-Sequoia or Homebrew-only macOS installations, the hooks can skip credential-read, network-egress, filesystem-boundary, and MCP-write controls. Native deny rules independently protect some credential paths but do not backstop the egress or MCP controls. An attacker who can influence a prompt, repository, or evaluation flow can use the skipped checks to expose secrets or perform unauthorized tool actions. This issue is fixed in version 3.69.1.

context: isomorphic-git is a pure JavaScript implementation of Git for Node.js and browsers. Prior to 1.38.7, tree-entry validation in src/models/GitTree.js does not reject the Windows NTFS reserved pathname alias .git::$INDEX_ALLOCATION. When clone() or checkout materializes an attacker-controlled tree containing this alias on Windows using an NTFS filesystem, the alias resolves to the active .git directory and permits writes to trusted repository metadata instead of a normal worktree directory. A malicious repository or object stream can therefore poison repository configuration, hooks, refs, attributes, or other gitdir state. Strict hosting that rejects hasDotgit objects can block the crafted tree, and non-NTFS systems do not interpret the pathname as the active gitdir. isomorphic-git performs the gitdir write but does not itself execute the written hook or configuration; a later native Git or compatible-tool action, such as processing a poisoned core.fsmonitor value, can execute configured commands as the victim developer or CI identity. This issue is fixed in version 1.38.7.

context: mcp-ssh-manager is an MCP server for managing servers over SSH with human approval, an encrypted vault, and a live audit trail. Prior to 3.6.7, ssh_db_list, ssh_db_dump, ssh_db_import, and ssh_db_restore in src/database-manager.js interpolate caller-controlled database, table, collection, file path, user, host, port, and password values into shell-evaluated command strings without neutralization. Shell metacharacters in these arguments therefore execute arbitrary commands on the configured SSH target as the account used by the MCP server. ssh_db_list is classified as read-only and remains available in readonly and restricted server security modes, so this path bypasses the command-execution boundary those modes are intended to enforce. The dump and import builders are blocked in readonly mode but remain vulnerable in the default unrestricted mode. The earlier version 3.6.5 hardening covered only ssh_db_query query text; it did not protect the list, dump, import, or restore builders, or the connection flags used by query builders. This issue is fixed in version 3.6.7.

context: pmo-platform is a modular PMO and release-management platform for Claude Code. Prior to 3.73, core/hooks/block-fragile-refs.sh and core/hooks/block-gh-path-leak.sh source co-shipped awk primitives from core/hooks/lib/ and degrade when a required primitive is absent. In a partial or corrupted deployment, block-gh-path-leak.sh skips its entire path-leak check, while block-fragile-refs.sh skips only the positional-issue-reference detector and continues running its other detectors. Both hooks operate in a warning posture, so the impact is a skipped warning rather than bypass of an enforcing control, with no established exfiltration or code-execution primitive. This issue is fixed in version 3.73.

context: pmo-platform is a modular PMO and release-management platform for Claude Code. Prior to 3.73, release/skills/pmo-skill-refiner/eval-viewer/generate_review.py and viewer.html contain three security weaknesses in the local evaluation viewer. During workspace scanning and generation, _find_runs_recursive and build_run follow symlinks and embed_file reads their targets without confining resolved paths to the workspace, although the server do_GET path is not a traversal surface. embed_file also reads output files without a size cap or redaction, allowing secrets or personally identifiable information to be embedded in a no-auth locally served page or shareable static file. Separately, do_POST /api/feedback writes caller-supplied JSON without authentication, an Origin check, or a cross-site request forgery token, allowing a malicious page or DNS-rebound localhost target to modify feedback while the server runs. This issue is fixed in version 3.73.

context: A vulnerability was found in RPM's rpmbuild tarball processing. When processing a crafted source archive, the getTarSpec() function in tools/rpmbuild.cc passes an attacker-controlled tar archive member name to rpmExpand() as part of a %{basename:...} macro expression. A specially crafted .spec member name can therefore inject RPM macros, including Lua expressions, resulting in arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the user running rpmbuild. This can be exploited when a victim or automated build system processes an attacker-controlled source tarball using rpmbuild tarball mode (such as -ts, -ta, or -tb).

context: SportEase is a web application for managing school sports events, class rosters, and competition teams. Prior to 1.3, an authenticated account with is_profile_complete=false can submit an attacker-selected class_id for any class in the currently active event to PUT /api/user/profile during first profile completion. AuthHandler.UpdateProfile accepts the class without validating the user's legitimate membership and automatically derives and assigns the corresponding {class_name}_rep role while isFirstCompletion is true. The attacker can become representative of one selected class, view roster information including email addresses, and add or remove competition-team assignments. Downstream handlers correctly reject access to other classes, so the impact is bounded to the selected class, but the representative privilege cannot be revoked through the exposed API and requires direct database intervention or another out-of-band remediation method. This issue is fixed in version 1.3.

context: rclone versions >= v1.72.0 and <= v1.74.4 (fixed in v1.75.0) contain multiple denial-of-service vulnerabilities in the archive backend's SquashFS parser, which relies on the github.com/diskfs/go-diskfs dependency. The parser fails to validate attacker-controlled superblock and metadata values before use. An attacker who can place or modify a SquashFS image in storage exposed through an rclone :archive: remote can craft a malicious image that triggers an integer division-by-zero panic (zero block size), an out-of-bounds slice panic (out-of-range inode metadata offset), or a non-progress CPU loop (truncated metadata stream). Variants 1 and 2 terminate the rclone process and, via 'rclone serve sftp', can crash the entire SFTP server; variant 3 causes sustained CPU consumption. Parsing is lazy, so a victim or remote client must address or descend into the malicious archive object to trigger it.

context: The BuddyBoss Addons plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Authentication Bypass leading to Account Takeover in versions up to, and including, 1.2.1. This is due to the Social Login REST endpoint trusting unverified Apple and Facebook identity-token claims and linking an attacker-controlled provider identifier to an existing WordPress user selected by the token’s email claim. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers who know a user’s email address to associate their provider identity with that account, including administrator accounts, and subsequently authenticate as the victim. Successful exploitation requires the BuddyBoss Platform plugin to be installed and active, with the Social Login module and selected provider enabled and configured. On sites with the separate BuddyBoss App JWT component, the vulnerable REST request can return an application token immediately.

context: The proxy middleware in mcp-use's inspector forwards requests to a destination the caller names. mountMcpProxy in libraries/typescript/packages/mcp-use/src/server/middleware/mcp-proxy.ts read the target from the X-Target-URL header or the __mcp_target parameter and proxied to it without inspecting the host, so loopback, link-local and private addresses were all accepted, as were names that resolve to them, and the validation was not reapplied to a redirect the destination returned. A caller could therefore make the server issue requests to addresses reachable only from the host it runs on and read the responses. In mcp-use 2.x the proxy moved to the @mcp-use/inspector package, whose mcp-proxy.ts calls isSafeProxyTarget, which checks the resolved address against private, loopback and link-local ranges before proxying and bounds the number of redirects followed.

context: ToolUniverse ran caller-supplied Python inside a sandbox that could be escaped, on a server that required no authentication. The executor behind the python_code_executor tool, in python_executor_tool.py, inspected the submitted source for a denied list of attribute names and calls but left the attribute-lookup builtins available and did not stop a dunder attribute reached through a string lookup or through a module already permitted, so a caller could walk from a literal's class to its base and enumerate subclasses to obtain a reference to the process and subprocess modules. A per-call argument also let the caller widen the import allow-list before the inspection ran. The HTTP and MCP servers in http_api_server.py and smcp_server.py bound to every interface with debugging enabled and no authentication, so any caller able to reach the port executed code as the server process. context: The Telnyx MCP server exposed its HTTP transport on every interface and did not require a caller credential. packages/mcp-server/src/http.ts served MCP on the root path with a listener bound to all interfaces and parsed the caller's authentication headers in a mode that did not fail when they were absent, so a request without any credential completed initialisation and dispatched tools. Dispatch forwarded the server's own stored credentials, the Telnyx API key and client secret together with the code-execution key, to the upstream endpoint, so an unauthenticated caller able to reach the port acted with them. The current code defaults the host to loopback, requires a server API key, and enforces it in middleware.

context: A flaw was found in libsolv, a dependency-resolution library used by RPM-based package managers such as dnf and zypper to work with .solv repository cache files. When libsolv rewrites a .solv cache file, it reads directory-id values from the file's compressed filelist data without validating that they fall within the expected range. A corrupted or specially crafted .solv cache file (for example, one left in a torn state after an unclean system shutdown) can cause an out-of-bounds memory write when a tool such as dnf, yum, or zypper next processes it. Successful exploitation is expected to result in a crash of the affected tool (denial of service); it is not expected to allow arbitrary code execution because the out-of-bounds write always stores a fixed, non-attacker-controlled value.

context: The GiveWP – Donation Plugin and Fundraising Platform plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to donor account account takeover in all versions up to, and including, 4.17.0. This is due to the plugin not properly validating a donor's identity prior to updating the password of a linked WordPress account. The donation receipt processes an attacker-controlled first name through the V3 template engine and then reprocesses the result through the legacy `{meta_donor_*}` engine, which can disclose the donor's email-access bearer token. The donor-dashboard password endpoint accepts that token by itself and calls `wp_set_password()` for the WordPress user linked to the donor. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to reset the password of any WordPress account linked to a GiveWP donor record and gain access to that account. If the linked account is an administrator, the attacker can achieve full site compromise and remote code execution through standard administrator functionality. A published GiveWP form with a usable gateway, enabled donor email access (enabled by default), knowledge of the donor email address, and an account already linked to the targeted donor record are required. NOTE: This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-82676 to satisfy the administrator donor pre-requisite for a targeted administrator user attack.

context: Traefik versions >= v3.7.0 and < v3.7.11 contain an authentication bypass in the Kubernetes Ingress NGINX provider. context: isomorphic-git is a pure JavaScript implementation of Git for Node.js and browsers. Prior to 1.38.8, git cherry-pick applies tree changes through applyTreeChanges in src/utils/walkerToTreeEntryMap.js without checking whether a leading path component is a symbolic link. If a victim worktree contains a tracked symlink to a location outside the worktree and a cherry-picked tree places a file beneath that path, the write follows the symlink and materializes attacker-controlled blob content at the external destination. This allows arbitrary file writes and can cause data tampering, code injection into interpreted files, privilege escalation, denial of service, or follow-on code execution depending on the selected target path. This issue is fixed in version 1.38.8.

context: Snipe-IT versions 4.2.0 through 8.6.3 expose Laravel Passport's auto-registered personal-access-token routes (GET, POST, DELETE /oauth/personal-access-tokens*) with only 'web' and 'auth:web' middleware, without the self.api permission gate that Snipe-IT enforces on its own token endpoints (/account/api and /api/v1/account/personal-access-tokens). context: Snipe-IT 8.5.0 through 8.6.3 contains an open redirect vulnerability in its SAML assertion-consumer endpoint (SamlController::acs, POST /saml/acs). The endpoint wrote the RelayState POST parameter directly into Laravel's url.intended session key with only CR/LF characters stripped, and LoginController later issued redirect()->intended(), which passes an absolute URL through to the Location header unchanged. An unauthenticated attacker who induces a user of a SAML-SSO-enabled instance to visit a crafted IdP-initiated SSO link can therefore cause the victim's browser to be redirected to an arbitrary absolute external URL immediately after a successful authentication, which the advisory notes facilitates credential-harvesting phishing. No account on the target instance and no compromise of the identity provider are required. Only deployments with SAML SSO enabled are affected. Fixed in 8.7.0 (commit d30b73d, PR #19386), which validates RelayState via a new Helper::sameOriginUrl check before storing it.

context: Snipe-IT versions >= 7.0.12 and <= 8.6.3 contain an authorization bypass in the Livewire importer component (App\Livewire\Importer, mounted at the imports.index route). The component only checked the broad 'import' ability at mount time, while its files() and activeFile() computed properties queried the imports table with no owner or company scope. As a result, any authenticated non-superuser holding the import permission could view every Import record on the instance (original filename, file_path, filesize, import_type and creation timestamp) and could invoke the selectFile($id) Livewire action with any auto-incrementing Import ID to load another user's record, exposing its stored preview data (header_row column headers and first_row, the first data row of the CSV). Because import CSVs commonly contain personal data, asset serial numbers and license keys, this discloses sensitive information; in Full Multiple Companies Support (FMCS) deployments the disclosure also crosses company/tenant boundaries. Impact is limited to preview data rather than the full CSV file, and superusers were unaffected. Fixed in version 8.7.0, which scopes non-superuser reads to imports owned by the caller.

context:
When Apache Shiro is used with the Jakarta EE integration module, the automatic form saving feature weakens the security of a form that is resubmitted after login.
Cookies set by the application during the resubmission could lose their security attributes, such as `Secure` and `SameSite`.
In addition, the resubmitted form data and cookies could be sent to an untrusted host.
This issue affects Apache Shiro from 2.0.0-alpha through 3.0.1, only when using `shiro-jakarta-ee` integration module with form saving enabled (the default).

Mitigation: Upgrade to version 3.0.2 or later, which no longer replays the form over the network, and avoids this class of issues entirely.
Alternatively, you can set the `org.apache.shiro.form-resubmit-host` (String) and `org.apache.shiro.form-resubmit-port` (Integer) system properties to restrict the host and port that Shiro will connect to when resubmitting a form.

context: Traefik is a HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In versions >= v3.7.0 and <= v3.7.11, the Kubernetes ingress-nginx provider mishandles Ingresses that carry both an authentication annotation and the nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/from-to-www-redirect annotation. For such Ingresses the provider creates an additional 'sibling' router that matches on the host alone, carries only the RedirectRegex middleware, and still points at the parent router's protected backend service. Because RedirectRegex is not a terminal handler, a request its pattern does not match is forwarded to the backend, and because the redirect pattern only accepts a numeric port while Traefik's host matcher canonicalizes the authority via net.SplitHostPort, a request with a non-numeric or empty port (for example 'Host: www.example.com:x') selects the sibling router, misses the redirect, and is proxied to the protected backend with none of the Ingress's annotation-derived middlewares applied. This discards not only authentication (e.g. BasicAuth) but every annotation-derived middleware, including source-IP allowlisting. Traefik v2 and v3 releases before v3.7.0 are not affected. The issue is fixed in v3.7.12.

context: Traefik is an HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In versions >= v2.8.2 through <= v2.11.55 and >= v3.0.0 through <= v3.7.11, the entryPoints.<name>.transport.respondingTimeouts settings — notably readTimeout, which is enabled by default at 60s — are not applied to the HTTP/3 request path. readTimeout is enforced as a deadline on the underlying TCP connection, which cannot be applied to a QUIC stream, and Traefik's HTTP/3 server is constructed without any timeout. As a result, on entry points with HTTP/3 enabled, an unauthenticated remote client that trickles request body bytes can hold a request open indefinitely and, with it, one upstream connection per request, exhausting bounded backend connection pools and causing denial of service. The issue was introduced in v2.8.2 when a quic-go API change removed the embedded http.Server that carried these timeouts. Fixed in v2.11.56 and v3.7.12.

context: Traefik is an HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In Traefik v1.x, v2.x through v2.11.55, and v3.0.0 through v3.7.11, header names are canonicalized only on dashes, so X-Auth-User, X_Auth_User and X.Auth.User are treated as three distinct headers by Traefik, while backends that derive variable names from header names (CGI, WSGI, PHP, NGINX and others) collapse them into a single variable. A client can therefore smuggle a dot-form alias of a header that Traefik manages past the middleware managing it — for example supplying X.Authenticated.User alongside the canonical X-Authenticated-User written by the ForwardAuth middleware — causing such a backend to read the client-supplied value instead of the identity Traefik asserted. In the tested configuration (PHP 8.2 built-in SAPI over an HTTP/1 backend path), Go's lexical header ordering makes the attacker-supplied value win deterministically, so a client that ForwardAuth admits as a low-privilege identity can be treated by the backend as a different user or role. Any header Traefik sets is affected, not only ForwardAuth's. This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-x677-9fxg-v5c5, which blocked only the underscore form. Fixed in v2.11.56 and v3.7.12, which add the aliasHeadersStrategy entry-point option; because it defaults to 'keep' for backwards compatibility, it must be explicitly set to 'delete' or 'reject' for the fix to take effect. nvd.description: Traefik is an HTTP reverse proxy and load balancer. In Traefik v1.x, v2.x through v2.11.55, and v3.0.0 through v3.7.11, header names are canonicalized only on dashes, so X-Auth-User, X_Auth_User and X.Auth.User are treated as three distinct headers by Traefik, while backends that derive variable names from header names (CGI, WSGI, PHP, NGINX and others) collapse them into a single variable. A client can therefore smuggle a dot-form alias of a header that Traefik manages past the middleware managing it — for example supplying X.Authenticated.User alongside the canonical X-Authenticated-User written by the ForwardAuth middleware — causing such a backend to read the client-supplied value instead of the identity Traefik asserted. In the tested configuration (PHP 8.2 built-in SAPI over an HTTP/1 backend path), Go's lexical header ordering makes the attacker-supplied value win deterministically, so a client that ForwardAuth admits as a low-privilege identity can be treated by the backend as a different user or role. Any header Traefik sets is affected, not only ForwardAuth's. This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-x677-9fxg-v5c5, which blocked only the underscore form. Fixed in v2.11.56 and v3.7.12, which add the aliasHeadersStrategy entry-point option; because it defaults to 'keep' for backwards compatibility, it must be explicitly set to 'delete' or 'reject' for the fix to take effect. Unmaintained release lines will not receive a patch.

context: Grav is a flat-file CMS. In Grav 1.7.0 before 1.7.53.3 and 2.0.0 before 2.0.22, when the debugger is enabled (system.debugger.enabled: true, which is not the default), the Clockwork profiler endpoint is exposed without authentication: InitializeProcessor::handleDebuggerRequest() intercepts any path containing /__clockwork/ during bootstrap and passes it to Debugger::debuggerRequest(), which performs no user lookup, IP restriction, or Clockwork authenticator check, and also supports anonymous pagination over the entire stored history. With the shipped censored: false default, each stored record contains raw request cookies (including Grav's session cookie, whose value is the PHP session id, allowing an attacker to resume another user's session, including an authenticated admin's), the full parsed request body (Grav's login form posts data[username]/data[password], so passwords are stored in plaintext because Clockwork's password filter only inspects top-level keys), and the site's entire system and plugin configuration, including operator-saved secrets such as SMTP credentials, third-party API keys, and licence keys. Authorization and X-API-Token headers are stored even when censored: true. On Grav 2.0, setting provider: debugbar does not avoid the issue because Grav forces the Clockwork provider for requests preferring a JSON response. The issue is fixed in 1.7.53.3 and 2.0.22, which restrict /__clockwork/ to server-local requests or requests presenting the new system.debugger.token secret and strip cookies and credential headers from stored records. Workarounds include setting debugger.enabled: false or blocking /__clockwork/ at the web server or CDN.

context: The urwid web display backend (urwid/display/web.py) generates web session identifiers (urwid_id) in Screen.start() by concatenating two random.randrange(10**9) calls that use Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG, which is not cryptographically secure. Each call consumes approximately 30 bits of PRNG state, and the Mersenne Twister internal state is approximately 19,937 bits, so an attacker who observes approximately 334 session IDs (for example via the X-Urwid-ID HTTP response header) can fully reconstruct the internal state and predict all past and future session IDs (Path B). The same identifier is also used as the filename of a FIFO created in the world-listable /tmp directory (for example /tmp/urwid375487765176907690.in), so any local user on the host can list /tmp to enumerate active session tokens directly (Path A). With a valid session ID, an attacker can read the victim's terminal screen via the polling endpoint, inject keystrokes into the victim's session (yielding OS-level code execution with the session owner's privileges if the session runs a shell), and inject exit sequences or flood the FIFO to terminate or crash the session. A prior Bandit S311 warning on this usage was suppressed with # noqa: S311 rather than fixed

context: NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. context: NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. From 4.5.00 until 4.6.01, an authenticated settings-module administrator can upload a PKCS#12 S/MIME certificate whose X.509 Subject CN contains path separators and traversal components. The smimeadd handler in admin/settings/smtp.php applies only an at-sign replacement before using the CN in .key, .crt, and .pem paths beneath data/certs. context: NukeViet CMS is a multi Content Management System. Prior to 4.5.12 and 4.6.02, an attacker who can reach an image-upload flow can upload a valid image with appended PHP short-tag code and a double-extension filename. context:
Issue summary: Receiving crafted out-of-sequence DTLS handshake fragments may
cause OpenSSL to allocate a full message-length reassembly buffer for each
buffered message, so a small amount of wire data consumes a large amount of
memory.

Impact summary: A remote attacker can send a few small crafted DTLS handshake
fragments to make a DTLS server or client allocate well over a megabyte of
memory per connection, which may lead to memory exhaustion and Denial of
Service if many connections are made.

CWE: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

Description: DTLS handshake messages can arrive out of order and fragmented,
so OpenSSL buffers fragments of up to ten out-of-sequence messages until
reassembly is possible. When the first fragment of a new message arrives,
OpenSSL allocates a buffer sized to the full message length declared in the
fragment header, plus a reassembly bitmap, instead of storing only the bytes
actually received. The declared length is capped by the maximum certificate
list size, 128KB by default, and that cap applies to every handshake message
type rather than only to Certificate messages.

Only DTLS endpoints reach this code. TLS, QUIC and applications that do not
use DTLS are unaffected. An attacker sends fragments that declare a large
message length but carry almost no data, using up to ten distinct message
sequence numbers.

A single connection can then hold roughly 1.4MB of buffers from about 156
bytes on the wire. Because the number of buffered messages is capped, memory
exhaustion requires many connections or many peers, which is why the severity
is Low.

FIPS impact: no
The affected code is outside the FIPS module boundary.

context:
The IPv6 Neighbor Discovery code in subsys/net/ip/ipv6_nbr.c flushes a neighbour's queued packets at the end of handle_ra_input(). The Source Link-Layer Address Option (SLLAO) is optional in a Router Advertisement; when it is absent, handle_ra_input() still obtains (or creates) a neighbour cache entry for the RA source via net_ipv6_nbr_add() with a NULL link-layer address, so the entry stays in NET_IPV6_NBR_STATE_INCOMPLETE with nbr->idx == NET_NBR_LLADDR_UNKNOWN. The pending-packet drain loop was entered unconditionally for that unresolved entry.

Each net_send_data() in the drain loop runs synchronously into net_ipv6_prepare_for_send(), which finds the neighbour still unresolved and hands the packet to net_ipv6_send_ns(), which puts it straight back onto the same pending_queue. The loop therefore never sees an empty queue. With a single queued packet it transmits a fresh Neighbor Solicitation on every iteration; with two or more queued packets it rotates the queue with no allocation and no transmission at all. The loop runs in the network RX thread with the global IPv6 neighbour mutex held.

An unauthenticated attacker on the same link can trigger this deterministically: advertise itself as a router, induce the victim to queue off-link traffic toward that router (for example by sending echo requests with an off-link source address) while leaving the solicitation unanswered, then send a second Router Advertisement without an SLLAO option. Spoofing an SLLAO-less RA from the legitimate router's link-local address has the same effect whenever traffic is queued for it. Router Advertisements are processed with no authentication whenever CONFIG_NET_IPV6_ND is enabled, which is the default for IPv6-capable builds.

The result is a permanent denial of service: the RX thread spins forever holding the neighbour lock, so all IPv6 transmission and every other user of the neighbour cache blocks, and the Neighbor Advertisement that would resolve the entry can no longer be processed. The ipv6_ns_reply_timer work item that would normally drop the pending packets also blocks on the same mutex. In the single-packet variant the loop additionally floods the link with Neighbor Solicitations. The fix restricts the flush to resolved entries (nbr->idx != NET_NBR_LLADDR_UNKNOWN), leaving the packets queued for the NS reply timeout. There is no memory-safety impact.

context:
net_if_ipv4_addr_rm() and net_if_ipv6_addr_rm() in subsys/net/ip/net_if.c unconditionally called net_if_addr_unref() on the target address. When an earlier removal could not complete because another subsystem still held a reference (the TCP stack takes one on the local address of every connection, in tcp_conn_new() and on connect()), the address is left in place with is_added cleared and is_used still set. A second removal of such an address decremented the reference count again, consuming a reference owned by that other holder. When it was the last one, the address slot was released, its NET_EVENT_IPV*_ADDR_DEL event fired, and the slot became reusable while the holder still believed it owned a reference.

Every address lookup helper matches on is_used and not on is_added, so a half-removed address stays visible to the rest of the stack and repeat removals are readily reachable from remote input. Under IPv6 SLAAC, an on-link node that sends a Router Advertisement with a short valid lifetime causes the address to expire into the deferred state; a refreshing Router Advertisement is handled by net_if_ipv6_addr_update_lifetime(), which re-arms the lifetime timer without restoring the reference, so the next expiry performs the second, reference-stealing removal. With CONFIG_NET_IPV4_ACD and DHCPv4, repeated spoofed ARP conflicts for the device's lease drive dhcpv4_acd_event_handler() into calling net_if_ipv4_addr_rm() more than once on the same address. Where CONFIG_USERSPACE is enabled, the net_if_ipv4_addr_rm_by_index() and net_if_ipv6_addr_rm_by_index() system calls let an unprivileged user-mode thread trigger the same kernel-side release deterministically.

The impact is loss of a configured IP address while connections are still using it, and a corrupted reference count that propagates: the slot can be handed to a newly added address, and when the stale holder later tears down, net_if_addr_unref() resolves the address by value and drops the new incarnation's only reference, removing a live address a second time. The affected objects are static array slots and the counter is never decremented below zero, so there is no memory corruption or information disclosure; the consequence is denial of service against the device's network connectivity, repeatable at the attacker's pace.

The fix resolves the address before touching the reference count and returns false without calling net_if_addr_unref() when the address is already marked as removed, so the public removal API can no longer consume a reference it does not own.

With CONFIG_NET_IPV4_ACD and DHCPv4, repeated spoofed ARP conflicts for the device's lease drive dhcpv4_acd_event_handler() into calling net_if_ipv4_addr_rm() more than once on the same address. Where CONFIG_USERSPACE is enabled, the net_if_ipv4_addr_rm_by_index() and net_if_ipv6_addr_rm_by_index() system calls let an unprivileged user-mode thread trigger the same kernel-side release deterministically.

The impact is loss of a configured IP address while connections are still using it, and a corrupted reference count that propagates: the slot can be handed to a newly added address, and when the stale holder later tears down, net_if_addr_unref() resolves the address by value and drops the new incarnation's only reference, removing a live address a second time. The affected objects are static array slots and the counter is never decremented below zero, so there is no memory corruption or information disclosure; the consequence is denial of service against the device's network connectivity, repeatable at the attacker's pace.

The fix resolves the address before touching the reference count and returns false without calling net_if_addr_unref() when the address is already marked as removed, so the public removal API can no longer consume a reference it does not own.

The SMSC911x/LAN9220 Ethernet driver stages every outgoing frame in a fixed-size static buffer before pushing it to the controller FIFO. eth_tx() in drivers/ethernet/eth_smsc911x.c took the frame length from net_pkt_get_len(pkt) and passed it directly to net_pkt_read(pkt, tx_buf, total_len), with no comparison against the size of tx_buf (NET_ETH_MAX_FRAME_SIZE). net_pkt_read() takes no destination size and only fails when the packet is shorter than the requested length, so any packet longer than the staging buffer was copied past its end.

Nothing between the IP layer and the driver bounds the frame to what the link can carry: ethernet_send() in subsys/net/l2/ethernet/ethernet.c performs no length check, and the IPv6 output path only compares the packet against the interface MTU when CONFIG_NET_IPV6_FRAGMENT is enabled (it is disabled by default). The size the stack will build is therefore governed by the interface MTU, and that MTU is remotely settable: handle_ra_input() in subsys/net/ip/ipv6_nbr.c honours the MTU option of any Router Advertisement with a value up to 0xffff, gated only by the standard hop-limit-255 and link-local-source checks. An unauthenticated attacker on the same link can raise the MTU and then have the device emit a single frame of several kilobytes, for example as a TCP segment from any service that returns more than ~1.5 KB or as an oversized UDP datagram.

The result is an out-of-bounds write into .bss immediately after tx_buf, with the overrun length and much of its content derived from the transmitted frame. Consequences range from corruption of adjacent kernel data and a crash to potential control-flow influence where the clobbered globals hold pointers; the practical overrun size is bounded by the network buffer pool rather than by the advertised MTU. The fix rejects frames larger than NET_ETH_MAX_FRAME_SIZE with -EMSGSIZE before any TX_DATA_PORT write, so the controller FIFO is also not left holding a command word without its payload.

The IPv6 neighbour discovery code in subsys/net/ip/ipv6_nbr.c keeps packets that are waiting for address resolution on a per-neighbour pending queue. A queued packet holds two references: the one handed over by the sender and a second one taken by net_ipv6_send_ns() when the packet is put on the queue. The Router Advertisement handler handle_ra_input() popped each packet off the queue and passed it to net_send_data(), relying on a trailing nbr_clear_ns_pending() call to release the queue reference — but that call then found the queue already empty and released nothing, so one reference was leaked for every pending packet flushed on an RA.

Router Advertisements are unauthenticated link-local ICMPv6 messages, so any node on the same link can trigger the flush. An attacker can make the leak deterministic by advertising itself as a router without a source link-layer address option, so the victim's neighbour entry stays INCOMPLETE, then inducing the victim to transmit through that next hop (the packet is queued and a neighbour solicitation is sent), leaving the solicitation unanswered and sending a further RA to drain the queue. Each round leaks one struct net_pkt together with its net_buf chain.

Leaked packets are never returned to the fixed-size pools, so the loss is permanent for the lifetime of the boot. With CONFIG_NET_PKT_TX_COUNT defaulting to 4 (14 with CONFIG_NET_PKT_LARGE_DEFAULTS), a small number of repetitions exhausts the transmit packet slab and the node stops being able to send any traffic. The impact is availability only: the reference count is always too high, never too low, so no use-after-free or memory corruption arises.

The fix moves the flush into a helper, nbr_send_pending(), which releases the queue reference for every packet it takes off the queue before handing the remaining reference to net_send_data(), and releases that one too if the send is refused.

context:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: rebind completed CREATE replays without draining the old channel

A completed DurableHandleReqV2 CREATE can be replayed through another
channel while its original channel is exiting. The existing replay path
returns the open but leaves its connection and oplock references pointing
at the old channel. Its open count also stays on that channel, and a
later CLOSE through the surviving channel decrements the wrong counter.

After checking the owner, lease key and persistent flag, verify that an
active open is still published in the requesting session's file table.
Do this even when no oplock was granted, and before processing a consumed
replay. Do not read a borrowed opinfo session pointer for this check.

Keep a healthy original binding. If the original channel is exiting or
releasing, move the open and its own oplock references to the requesting
channel. Serialize this with CLOSE using the session file-table lock,
and with detach, reconnect and notification snapshots using m_lock.
The earlier lock index and lease-table changes make their lifetimes
independent of this connection change. No old-channel r_count wait is
needed, including when an unrelated request remains active there.

Account final close against fp->conn in one place, balance durable detach
and reconnect, and transfer the count with a replay binding change. A
final global lookup put may run after CLOSE has removed the volatile id;
unlink the open from the inode list on that final close as well.

A live completed CREATE replay may follow a break that lowered the
durable open's batch oplock. Apply the batch eligibility check only to
detached reconnects, while retaining the owner, lease key and persistent
flag checks for active replays.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: guest_memfd: take the invalidate lock when unbinding a dying file

kvm_gmem_unbind() takes mapping->invalidate_lock only if the
get_file_active() succeeds. When the guest_memfd file is dying, its
reference count is already zero so get_file_active fails and the binding
is removed without holding the invalidate lock.

kvm_gmem_invalidate_{start,end}() checks f->bindings independently to
decide whether to begin or end KVM MMU invalidation. So, the bindings
must therefore remain stable between the two calls. Otherwise, unbind
can remove a binding after start increments mmu_invalidate_in_progress,
but before end finds the binding and decrements it.
Example, unbind race with memory failure:

  CPU 0: memory failure               CPU 1: memslot delete
  ----------------------------------  ---------------------------
                                      (guest_memfd file is dying)
  kvm_gmem_error_folio()
    kvm_gmem_invalidate_start()
      finds binding
      mmu_invalidate_in_progress++
                                      kvm_gmem_unbind()
                                        get_file_active() fails
                                        removes binding
    kvm_gmem_invalidate_end()
      no binding found
      counter stays elevated

mmu_invalidate_retry() then returns 1 forever, so guest page faults
retry without ever installing a mapping and the guest hangs.

Remove the distinction between live and dying files in the unbind path.
Always use slot->gmem.file and take the invalidate lock when it's non-NULL.
Normal unbind callers hold slots_lock, which prevents release from clearing
the pointer or freeing the file state until unbind completes. Final VM
teardown can only see a NULL pointer because guest_memfd pins the KVM until
release has cleared all bindings.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86: Take SRCU in kvm_zap_gfn_range()

kvm_zap_gfn_range() walks memslots and rmaps and may drop mmu_lock to
reschedule. Callers that do not already hold kvm->srcu (or slots_lock)
can race with memslot deletion: synchronize_srcu_expedited() does not
wait, kvm_free_memslot() frees the old slot and its rmap, and the zap
resumes on freed memory.

The VFIO noncoherent-DMA path hits this by zapping the entire GPA
space without SRCU. KASAN reported:

  BUG: KASAN: vmalloc-out-of-bounds in slot_rmap_walk_next+0x82/0x1c0
  Read of size 8 at addr ffffc900005c1008
  Call Trace:
   slot_rmap_walk_next+0x82/0x1c0
   __kvm_rmap_zap_gfn_range+0x17a/0x280
   kvm_zap_gfn_range+0x2a6/0x6a0
   kvm_vfio_set_attr+0x576/0x770
   kvm_device_ioctl+0x1ff/0x3b0

Take SRCU inside kvm_zap_gfn_range() so every caller is covered.
Nesting with an existing kvm->srcu critical section is fine; the
helper uses a local index. Drop the now-redundant SRCU pair from
__kvm_set_or_clear_apicv_inhibit().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: x86/mmu: Bug the VM if KVM attempts to walk more levels than the MMU has

Extend the "EFER.LMA && !CR4.PAE" check, which exists largely to guard
against KVM configuring a paging32 MMU with more than 2 levels of paging,
with a very explicit check for exactly that: that KVM isn't trying to walk
more levels of paging than the MMU template provides.  I.e. harden KVM
against all bugs that would cause KVM to generates accesses beyond the
bounds of guest_walker's arrays, regardless of how KVM ended up with the
misconfigured MMU.

Note, don't use w->cpu_role.base.level directly as the paging64 template
only provides two levels of page tables for PAE paging on 32-bit hosts, and
handles the third level by manually emulating the PDPTR access.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: nSVM: Reject KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE if L1 has EFER.LMA=1 && EFER.LME=0

Reject KVM_SET_NESTED_STATE if the incoming L1 host state has what is
effectively an impossible EFER combination of LMA=1 but LME=0, i.e. if the
state says long mode is active but not enabled.  Unlike VMX, SVM doesn't
have an explicit consistent check for the illegal combination; presumably
hardware simply ignores EFER.LMA if EFER.LME=0.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: SVM: Trigger new ASID allocation in both VMCBs on pCPU switch

When the pCPU where the VMCB was most recently used is switched, reset
the ASID generation in both VMCBs, triggering new ASID allocation for
the immediate VMRUN as well as the next VMRUN on the other VMCB.

The ASID is shared between vmcb01 and vmcb02, and gets flushed on every
nested transition. However, since pCPU tracking is done per VMCB, it is
possible for one VMCB to allocate a new ASID when migrated to a new
pCPU, and then the other VMCB reuses that ASID on the old pCPU. This can
result in the same ASID being used by multiple vCPUs on the old pCPU.

Example scenario:
- vCPU runs on pCPU A, vmcb01 is active, asid=1.
- vCPU migrates to pCPU B, vmcb01 pCPU changes, new asid=2.
- Another vCPU runs on pCPU A and allocates asid=2 as well.
- vCPU migrates back to pCPU A, and then switches to vmcb02 before it
  runs again with vmcb01.
- No pCPU switch is detected for vmcb02, so VMRUN is done with asid=2.
- Two vCPUs end up using asid=2 on the same pCPU.

Keep the VMCB dirtying to the active VMCB only. Clean bits are tracked
by a pCPU for each VMCB, so do not unnecessarily dirty a VMCB if its
pCPU does not change.

Additionally, initialize the tracked pCPU for vmcb02 to -1 on nested
enablement as hardening, so that a new ASID allocation is always
triggered when nested is disabled and re-enabled.

No performance regression was noticed when overcommitting L1 vCPUs in L0
(to force rescheduling), pinning L1 <-> L2 vCPUs, and running CPUID in a
tight loop bouncing between 2 vCPUs in L2.

An alternative (and perhaps more proper) fix would be tracking the ASID
per-VMCB instead (e.g. [1]). However, that's a more involved change, and
it would result in having different ASIDs for L1 and L2 without actually
properly maintaining them. It would probably work because all TLB
flushes target the current VMCB, and the other VMCB is always flushed on
nested transitions, but the code ends up in an arguably more fragile
state. Punt a proper clean fix to an incoming (and overdue) overhaul of
SVM's ASID usage [2].

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/20250205182402.2147495-2-yosry.ahmed@linux.dev
[2] https://lore.kernel.org/kvm/20260728003557.1136583-1-yosry@kernel.org

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

SUNRPC: fix oversized GSS proxy token copy

gss_read_proxy_verf() allocates one page per token chunk, but it copies the
entire linear head of an RPC request into in_token->pages[0]. A UDP datagram
can leave more than PAGE_SIZE bytes in the linear head, so a large
RPCSEC_GSS INIT token overwrites following pages.

Copy the linear head in page-sized chunks before switching to the request
page array. The linear head itself can span multiple pages.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

SUNRPC: Do not credit control-record octets to the RPC stream

svc_tcp_sock_recv_cmsg() receives up to two octets into a local
buffer, and returns that count for any record type other than
TLS_RECORD_TYPE_ALERT. Nothing reached the caller's buffer, but
svc_tcp_read_marker() adds the count to sk_tcplen and
svc_tcp_read_msg()'s caller adds it to sk_datalen. The RPC stream
advances over octets it never received. The fragment marker is
assembled from stale sk_marker octets. The message body comes from
pages nothing wrote.

A conforming client reaches this. RFC 8446 Section 4.6.3 lets either
peer send KeyUpdate once it has sent its Finished, and svcsock has no
rekey path. kTLS leaves the partially consumed record on ctx->rx_list,
so the body drains two octets per svc_tcp_recvfrom() call. Each pair
is credited the same way.

Return -EAGAIN for a record that is not an alert. That is what
svc_tcp_sock_process_cmsg()'s default arm returned before the receive
moved into a local buffer.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: preflight SEQUENCE replies before accepting a slot

nfsd4_sequence() narrows the reply buffer to the session's cached
reply limit before it accepts the slot seqid. A client may negotiate
ca_maxresponsesize_cached down to NFSD_MIN_HDR_SEQ_SZ, and
nfsd4_alloc_slot() then gives every slot a zero-length sl_data[]. A
COMPOUND tag can fill that narrowed buffer until it holds the
SEQUENCE opcode but not the status word that follows.
nfsd4_encode_operation() returns without running
nfsd4_encode_sequence(), so cstate.data_offset stays zero. It leaves
op->status at nfs_ok as well, so the COMPOUND is treated as having
succeeded.

nfsd4_store_cache_entry() declines to cache a lone SEQUENCE that
returned an error. That test reads the status the operation
reported, so it passes here. The copy starts at offset zero and
takes the whole reply, RPC and COMPOUND headers included, into the
zero-length sl_data[]. The COMPOUND tag is copied along with it, so
the client picks most of the bytes written past the end of the slot:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-out-of-bounds in read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390
  Write of size 80 at addr ffff888003a549cd by task kunit_try_catch/24
   __asan_memcpy+0x38/0x60
   read_bytes_from_xdr_buf+0x1bc/0x390
   nfsd4_sequence_done+0x5b0/0x810
   nfs4svc_encode_compoundres+0x1bf/0x240

Check that the fixed-size SEQUENCE result, plus room for a following
operation's error status, fits the negotiated limit before narrowing
the buffer and consuming the slot seqid. The slot and its reply
cache are left unchanged, as RFC 8881 Section 2.10.6.1.2 requires of
an error returned from SEQUENCE.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

nfsd: don't modify a session slot when replaying its cached reply

nfsd4_sequence() claims a session slot by setting NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE
under nn->client_lock. A reply served from the slot's reply cache does
not claim it, and that distinction lived only in cstate->status, which
nfsd4_sequence() set to nfserr_replay_cache. Commit cc028a10a48c
("NFSD: Hoist status code encoding into XDR encoder functions") moved
nfsd4_proc_compound()'s cstate->status assignment below the out:
label, and the replay path's goto out was the one path that relied on
skipping it. The test in nfsd4_sequence_done() therefore no longer
identifies a replay, and every replay now stores its reply and clears
NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE as though it owned the slot.

NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE is the interlock: check_slot_seqid() rejects every
sequence id for a slot that is in use, before replay_matches_cache()
runs. A replay never sets it, so two replays can be in flight on the
same slot at once. One can read slot->sl_cred under nn->client_lock
while the other's completion frees and rebuilds it from the XDR
encoder without that lock. Two completions can also collide with each
other and release the same group_info twice. free_svc_cred() leaves
cr_uid, cr_gid and cr_flavor intact, so the reader passes every
earlier test in same_creds() and dereferences a NULL cr_group_info.
From a 6.12.91 production server:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000000000000004
  CPU: 63 UID: 0 PID: 39015 Comm: nfsd
  RIP: 0010:same_creds+0x38/0xa0 [nfsd]
  RDX: 0000000000000000
  Call Trace:
   nfsd4_sequence+0x6a8/0x910 [nfsd]
   nfsd4_proc_compound+0x345/0x670 [nfsd]
   nfsd_dispatch+0x100/0x220 [nfsd]
   svc_process_common+0x311/0x700 [sunrpc]
   svc_process+0x131/0x1c0 [sunrpc]
   svc_recv+0x7ef/0x9c0 [sunrpc]
   nfsd+0xa3/0x100 [nfsd]
  Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception

Since v6.14 a live session's slot table can shrink, and the unowned
store becomes a use-after-free write. nfsd4_sequence() defers the
shrink while a slot is in use, but it tests NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE, which a
replay does not set, so free_session_slots() can kfree() the slot the
replay still holds in cstate->slot.

Record the claim in cstate->slot_owned when nfsd4_sequence() accepts a
request and test that in nfsd4_sequence_done(), so only the request
that claimed the slot updates its cached reply and clears
NFSD4_SLOT_INUSE. svc_generic_init_request() zeroes the compound
response before each request, so the flag starts clear.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

NFSD: copy SETXATTR data from all XDR buffer segments

nfsd4_vbuf_from_vector() manually copies the head followed by whole
pages starting at offset zero. This assumes that all remaining data
starts at the beginning of the page array and that no data is stored
in the tail.

However, nfsd4_decode_setxattr() passes an xdr_buf returned by
xdr_stream_subsegment(). Such a sub-buffer can have a nonzero
page_base and can span its page and tail segments. Ignoring that
layout can copy the wrong bytes into the value passed to
vfs_setxattr().

Use read_bytes_from_xdr_buf(), which observes the complete xdr_buf
layout.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate SMB1 EA list bounds before parsing

CIFSSMBQAllEAs() checks the server-provided EA list length by adding it
to the response pointer. On 32-bit systems, a positive length can wrap
the pointer and pass the comparison. The parser then walks outside the
received response while reading the next FEA header.

A response with a list length of 0x40000000 reproduces this as a native
i386 page fault and kernel panic from listxattr() against an SMB1
server.

Check that the EA list starts within the SMB byte area before reading
its header. Keep its length unsigned and compare it with the bytes left
in the response without pointer addition.

SMB1 is not negotiated by default and requires an explicit vers=1.0
mount.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate NT transaction response layout and offsets

validate_ntransact() assumes that the response uses the fixed 18-word NT
transaction layout. A different WordCount makes get_bcc() locate the byte
count at a different offset from pSMBr->ByteCount, allowing the subsequent
bounds checks to use inconsistent response boundaries.

The function also turns the 32-bit ParameterOffset and DataOffset fields
into pointers before checking their bounds. On a 32-bit client, a large
offset can wrap the pointer below end_of_smb and pass the one-sided pointer
comparison. The caller then dereferences the parameter pointer or copies
from the data pointer.

Require the expected WordCount before reading the byte count. Check each
offset and count against the received SMB length as integers before forming
either pointer. Use subtraction after validating the offset so that the
range checks cannot overflow.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: reclaim credits for decrypted reads with no matching mid

When a decrypted SMB2 READ response carries a MessageId that matches no
outstanding request, both the inline receive_encrypted_read() and the
offloaded smb2_decrypt_offload() paths drop the frame without accounting
the credits the server granted in it.  The plaintext unknown-frame path in
cifs_demultiplex_thread() already reclaims them with
smb2_add_credits_from_hdr(), so encrypted reads leak credits that the
plaintext path would not.

This also happens for legitimate frames - e.g. a reply that arrives after
the client has timed out and dropped the mid - so over a long-lived
connection the client's credit count drifts down and can eventually starve
it of the ability to issue requests.  The frame is AEAD-authenticated, so
the granted credits in the decrypted header come from the real server and
are safe to apply.

Reclaim the credits from the decrypted header before dropping the frame,
and export smb2_add_credits_from_hdr() so the SMB2 receive paths can use it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix buffer overflow in SMB2_tcon()

In SMB2_tcon(), unc_path is allocated with a fixed buffer size of
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH * 2 bytes (672 bytes). However, the user-controlled
UNC path (tree) length is passed to cifs_strtoUTF16(), which assumes the
destination buffer is large enough and writes strlen(tree) + 1 UTF-16 code
units.

Commit 62a1a439e0fd ("cifs: clean up handling of unc= option") removed the
length check on UNC mount options, allowing mount paths to exceed
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH while retaining the fixed-size buffer allocation in
SMB2_tcon(). Consequently, an oversized UNC string causes cifs_strtoUTF16()
to write past the end of the heap object, resulting in a slab-out-of-bounds
write. Furthermore, if a tree exceeds MAX_TREE_SIZE characters, strscpy()
truncates it in cifs_tcon::tree_name, causing subsequent reconnects or
failovers to fail.

Fix this by first verifying that the length of tree does not exceed
MAX_TREE_SIZE, returning -EINVAL if it does. Then, dynamically allocate
unc_path based on the length of tree so that it safely accommodates all
UTF-16 code units for paths within MAX_TREE_SIZE.

[pc: remove unused MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: fix buffer overflow in SMB2_tcon()

In SMB2_tcon(), unc_path is allocated with a fixed buffer size of
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH * 2 bytes (672 bytes). However, the user-controlled
UNC path (tree) length is passed to cifs_strtoUTF16(), which assumes the
destination buffer is large enough and writes strlen(tree) + 1 UTF-16 code
units.

Commit 62a1a439e0fd ("cifs: clean up handling of unc= option") removed the
length check on UNC mount options, allowing mount paths to exceed
MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH while retaining the fixed-size buffer allocation in
SMB2_tcon(). Consequently, an oversized UNC string causes cifs_strtoUTF16()
to write past the end of the heap object, resulting in a slab-out-of-bounds
write. Furthermore, if a tree exceeds MAX_TREE_SIZE characters, strscpy()
truncates it in cifs_tcon::tree_name, causing subsequent reconnects or
failovers to fail.

Fix this by first verifying that the length of tree does not exceed
MAX_TREE_SIZE, returning -EINVAL if it does. Then, dynamically allocate
unc_path based on the length of tree so that it safely accommodates all
UTF-16 code units for paths within MAX_TREE_SIZE.

[pc: remove unused MAX_SHARENAME_LENGTH]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: don't resurrect an exiting tcon from cached dir workers

cfids_laundromat_worker() bumps tcon->tc_count for every expired open
cfid and queues cached_dir_offload_close() without checking whether the
tcon is already being torn down.  Racing with the final cifs_put_tcon(),
the tcon comes back from zero and gets torn down twice:

  T1                                  T2
  cifs_put_tcon()
   --tc_count == 0, TID_EXITING
   tconInfoFree()
    free_cached_dirs()
     cancel_delayed_work_sync()       cfids_laundromat_worker()
                                       ++tc_count == 1
                                       queue_work(serverclose_wq)
    kfree(tcon->origin_fullpath)
    kfree(tcon)
                                      cached_dir_offload_close()
                                       close_cached_dir()  [UAF]
                                       cifs_put_tcon()
                                        tconInfoFree()     [double free]

cached_dir_lease_break() also bumps tc_count without tc_lock, racing with
the laundromat's locked update.

Take the tcon reference through a helper that refuses once the tcon is
TID_EXITING or its refcount has dropped to zero.  Queued put_work and
close_work then always hold a tcon reference, so tconInfoFree() can't
run before they finish and free_cached_dirs() doesn't need to flush any
workqueue.  If the laundromat can't get a reference, put the cfid back on
the dying list for free_cached_dirs() to free; its handle goes away with
the tree connection.

The lease break path finds the tcon on ses->tcon_list under
cifs_tcp_ses_lock, so it can't see TID_EXITING, but it now takes tc_lock.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: smbdirect: fix buffer length underflow in RDMA transfers

When a remote buffer descriptor is larger than the remaining local
buffer, smbdirect_connection_rdma_xmit() clamps its length and sets
buf_len to zero. The common accounting code then subtracts the clamped
length from buf_len, causing it to underflow. If another descriptor
follows, the loop processes it with a wrapped remaining length and
includes memory beyond the local buffer in the RDMA transfer.

A client can trigger an out-of-bounds kernel write with an SMB WRITE
request, or an out-of-bounds kernel read with an SMB READ request, by
supplying multiple RDMA buffer descriptors with an oversized descriptor
before the last one.

Remove the premature assignment to buf_len. Subtracting the clamped length
already consumes the remaining buffer, so the next iteration stops and
only descriptors within the local buffer are used to build work requests.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: server: size directory name conversion buffer correctly

A 2048-byte ASCII directory name needs 4098 bytes when converted to
UTF-16, including the terminator. ksmbd_convert_dir_info_name() caps
its allocation at PATH_MAX and writes past the end of that buffer.

Allocate space for one UTF-16 code unit per input byte plus the
terminator. Use kmalloc_array() to check the size calculation.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: bound inode fork length against the fork size during log recovery

xlog_recover_inode_commit_pass2() copies an inode log item's data/attr
fork region into the inode buffer using the on-log region length without
bounding it against the fork capacity, e.g.:

	len = item->ri_buf[2].iov_len;
	memcpy(XFS_DFORK_DPTR(dip), src, len);

The only guard is an ASSERT, which is a no-op on production kernels
(CONFIG_XFS_DEBUG off), and xfs_dinode_verify() runs only after the copy.
A crafted image with a dirty log can therefore drive a heap out-of-bounds
write at mount time. The XFS_ILOG_DBROOT sibling already passes
XFS_DFORK_DSIZE as a bound; the DDATA/DEXT and ADATA/AEXT memcpy paths
did not.

Bound each logged fork region against the destination fork size before
copying it, and reject the log item with -EFSCORRUPTED when it does not
fit. Because the recovered inode is only verified after the fork data has
been copied in, the checks are done up front, before any memcpy into the
on-disk inode.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: reject remote xattr entries with an out-of-range value length

xfs_attr3_leaf_verify_entry() validates a remote attribute entry's name
but never bounds its on-disk value length (xfs_attr_leaf_name_remote.
valuelen, a __be32). A crafted leaf with valuelen = 0x80000000 passes
the verifier and the CRC.

That length is later assigned into the signed int args->rmtvaluelen
(xfs_attr3_leaf_getvalue), becoming negative, which slips past the signed
-ERANGE check in xfs_attr_copy_value(); a getxattr() with a small buffer
then memcpy()s a full remote block into the small kvalue buffer
(xfs_attr_rmtval_copyout) -- a heap out-of-bounds write with
attacker-controlled content, from an unprivileged getxattr(2) on a
mounted crafted image.

Reject remote entries whose value length exceeds XFS_XATTR_SIZE_MAX in
the leaf verifier, so the malicious block is rejected at read time.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfs: reject out-of-range attribute value lengths in xfs_attr_copy_value

xfs_attr_copy_value() takes the value length as a signed int and, for a
remote xattr, is handed args->rmtvaluelen.  That field is filled from the
on-disk __be32 xfs_attr_leaf_name_remote.valuelen in
xfs_attr3_leaf_getvalue(), so a crafted length such as 0x80000000 is
stored into the signed rmtvaluelen as a negative number.

The "buffer too small" guard in xfs_attr_copy_value() is a signed
comparison:

	if (args->valuelen < valuelen)
		return -ERANGE;

A negative valuelen therefore compares as smaller than the caller's
buffer size, skips the -ERANGE path, and is then used as a copy length,
leading to an out-of-bounds copy of a full remote block into a small
getxattr(2) buffer on a mounted crafted image.

Reject a value length that is negative or larger than the maximum xattr
size before it is used, so a bogus on-disk length can no longer slip
through the value copier.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

rtnetlink: wait for RCU readers in rtnl_link_unregister()

rtnl_link_ops_get() finds ops on link_ops under rcu_read_lock() and only
then takes ops->srcu. rtnl_link_unregister() unlinks ops, then calls
synchronize_srcu() and cleanup_srcu_struct() without first waiting for
RCU readers. A reader that found ops before list_del_rcu() and has not yet
taken ops->srcu is not waited for.

Such a reader then locks a cleaned-up srcu_struct and keeps using ops
after the module that owns it is gone. rtnl_newlink() and
rtnl_dump_ifinfo() both look up ops without RTNL, the latter for any
user that dumps links filtered by kind.

With delays added between the lookup and srcu_read_lock() in
rtnl_link_ops_get(), and before rtnl_link_ops_put() in
rtnl_dump_ifinfo(), running "ip link show type dummy" alongside
"rmmod dummy" on a KASAN kernel gives:

  BUG: KASAN: vmalloc-out-of-bounds in __srcu_read_unlock+0x57/0x70
  Read of size 8 at addr ffffffffc02ff318 by task ip/147
  Call Trace:
   __srcu_read_unlock+0x57/0x70
   rtnl_dump_ifinfo.cold+0x30/0x3b
   rtnl_dumpit+0x7a/0x1b0
   netlink_dump+0x486/0x11b0
   __netlink_dump_start+0x661/0x910
   rtnetlink_rcv_msg+0x611/0x9e0
   netlink_rcv_skb+0x126/0x380
   netlink_unicast+0x605/0x830
   netlink_sendmsg+0x6d0/0xbb0
   __sys_sendto+0x335/0x3a0

Call synchronize_rcu() before synchronize_srcu(), as
rtnl_af_unregister() already does. This should be enough because
rtnl_link_ops_get() is the only RCU walker of link_ops, and it takes
ops->srcu before rcu_read_unlock(), so every reader that found ops is
covered by synchronize_srcu() once the RCU grace period ends. The extra
grace period only costs time at module unload.

Readers and the writer were serialized by RTNL until link_ops got its
own mutex, which is why the missing RCU wait did not matter before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: use the pinned upper dir in ovl_fix_origin()

Renames made directly on the upper filesystem during a lookup crash the
kernel.

A dentry that is passed to vfs_setxattr() must be pinned.
ovl_fix_origin() passes upper->d_parent to ovl_set_impure() without a
reference, and the lookup holds no lock of the upper directory. A
rename on the upper filesystem changes d_parent, and only the child
pins the new parent, so a second rename and an rmdir free it.

With delays in ovl_fix_origin() and ovl_set_impure(), renaming the upper
directory twice and removing the intermediate parent during the lookup
of a merge directory without an origin xattr gave a KASAN
use-after-free in vfs_setxattr().

Fix this by passing the upper dentry that the overlay parent holds.

[amir: add helper ovl_set_impure_dir()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: set OVL_WHITEOUTS before publishing the upper dir

Listing a directory while it is copied up causes a use-after-free of
the readdir cache.

A merge directory must never be iterated as a real upper directory:
that mode frees the cache in OVL_I(inode)->cache without looking at
its refcount, while files opened in merged mode still use it.
ovl_copy_up_workdir() publishes the upper dentry before it sets
OVL_WHITEOUTS, and ovl_dir_open() samples both without a lock, so an
open between the two stores finds the upper directory and takes it
for a real one.

With a delay between the two stores, an unprivileged process that
listed a directory during its copy-up saw only "." and "..", and its
next getdents freed the readdir cache of another descriptor.

Fix this by setting OVL_WHITEOUTS before ovl_inode_update(), so that
ovl_dir_reset() agrees with ovl_dir_open(), and by testing
OVL_TYPE_MERGE() of the path type in ovl_dir_open(), so that an open
that observes the upper dentry never iterates a merge dir as a real
dir, regardless of the order in which it observes the flag.

[amir: test OVL_TYPE_MERGE() instead of smp_rmb() in ovl_dir_open()]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ovl: hold a reference on the parent in readdir

Listing a directory on an overlay uses a freed dentry and crashes the
kernel when a lookup moves the directory at the same time.

Code that can sleep may only use d_parent without a reference while
something stops a move of the dentry. ovl_iterate_real(),
ovl_need_adjust_d_ino() and ovl_cache_update() use the d_parent of the
listed directory and hold only the lock of that directory. When a
lookup finds the directory under another parent after a change to a
layer, d_splice_alias() moves it without that lock and drops its
reference on the old parent.

With a delay in ovl_iterate_real(), getdents64 on an overlay directory
raced a rename in the lower layer and a lookup that moved its dentry,
and after an rmdir of the old parent KASAN reported a use-after-free in
security_inode_getattr().

Fix this by using dget_parent() in the three functions.

[amir: fix comments in ovl_need_adjust_d_ino()]
